lines: Clean feathers and straight shafts make trouble keep its distance.
A good bow <pulse>hears trouble</pulse> before the bell does.
A crooked feather makes a promise the arrow can't keep.
Distance changes everything. Trouble looks smaller until it arrives.
The best warning is the one that reaches trouble before trouble reaches us.
Aim is not just the hand. It is patience deciding not to flinch.
Most days, I am at the fletching table, trying to keep straight shafts from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think arrows is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good knife more than a loud promise. The knife has less to prove.
Good arrows start with straight thinking and end with careful hands.
Feathers look light until the aim depends on them.
A bow tells the truth about tension very quickly.
The smallest flaw gets louder after release.
I measure twice because the arrow only flies once.
String, shaft, feather, point, and then the patience to check it again.
People think aim begins in the eye. It usually begins in the breath.
A village with arrows ready can sleep a little closer to peace.
Wind is the kind of critic that never repeats itself fairly.
A good fletcher respects distance without trusting it.
The straightest arrow still needs someone steady behind it.
I have learned more from missed shots than easy ones.
A crooked shaft is honest early. A crooked plan waits.
The target never moves, which is more than I can say for danger.
Good work flies away and proves itself elsewhere.
That route you took me on flew about as straight as a warped arrow.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Following you taught me that plans sound much safer before anyone starts walking.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the road becomes a test of character.
I learned two things out there: stay close, and ask better questions earlier.
You move like danger is a normal part of the route. I am still adjusting to that.
It was not all bad. Some views are worth sore legs and nervous glances.
If I followed you again, I would pack more food and fewer assumptions.
